title: The chained woman
hookLine: a woman whose husband won't grant a divorce; every stream seeks solutions

cards: Rabbi Akiva is far from home, in Nehardea in Babylonia. A man there pulls him aside with a teaching he's been carrying.
In the land of Israel, he's heard, only one sage lets a woman remarry on the word of a single witness that her husband has died. Go back, the man says, and tell them in my name.
Akiva carries it home and repeats it before Rabban Gamaliel, and Gamaliel is glad. The Mishnah says the rule was then set: one witness is enough. Why would a court bend its own rules of evidence?

teach.b: Agunah. The word is usually translated the chained woman. In Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a document the husband gives.
The shadow side: without a get, she can't remarry under Jewish law.
First, the old case: the husband who vanished. A man goes to sea, or to war, and never comes back. No body, no document.
Is she a widow or a wife? Normally a court wants two witnesses. For her, the rabbis accepted one, and the Talmud gives the reason in a phrase: they were lenient because of the agunah.
The law bent to free her. Second, the modern case: the husband who refuses. He's alive, the marriage is over, and he won't give the get, sometimes to punish her, sometimes to bargain.
She's chained by his choice. Third, the answers, and each stream works in its own way.
In Orthodox communities, rabbinical courts can pressure a refusing husband, and some couples now sign a prenuptial agreement that makes refusal costly.
Conservative rabbis added a clause to the ketubah, and their courts have other tools.
Reform Judaism generally accepts a civil divorce, so this bind doesn't arise there in the same way.
And across the streams, women and rabbis have gone public, standing outside the homes and workplaces of men who refuse, asking them to give the get. Different paths, the same direction.
Akiva's single witness shows how the tradition's own rules can bend toward a woman who's waiting.

how: Orthodox couples may sign a halachic prenuptial agreement and rabbinical courts may press a husband to give a get; Conservative ketubot may include an added clause; Reform Judaism generally accepts civil divorce; and Jewish groups across the streams campaign for women who are refused a get.

games.q: you sit on a rabbinical court. a husband went to sea and never came back. one witness says he saw him die. normally you need two. what do you do?
o: wait for a second witness, however long it takes.
accept the one witness so she can remarry.
games.why: the Mishnah says the court set the rule that one witness is enough. the Talmud's reason: they were lenient because of the agunah.

practice: Hold in mind someone who feels trapped: a friend stuck in a job, a relative in a hard marriage, someone waiting on a decision another person won't make.

Don't try to fix it; just ask what one small key would look like, a call, a ride, a listening hour, the name of someone who can help. If anyone is in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help, any hour.

wordCard.voice: Agunah. The chained woman: a wife who cannot remarry because her husband has vanished or won't give a get. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a woman who cannot remarry because her husband is missing or refuses a get.

carryVoice: Your line: unchain her. The law has bent before, toward the one who waits. Rest well.
